dek: Daylight saving time ends Sunday, Nov. 1. What the science says about sleep, winter blues and what helps.

slides.label: The switch
slides.text: At *2 a.m. Sunday*, Nov. 1, clocks go back to 1 a.m. You get an extra hour of sleep, then sunset lands about *an hour earlier* on the clock for months.

slides.label: The adjustment
slides.text: The Sleep Foundation says the fall change is far less disruptive than the spring one. Most people adjust within *a few days to a few weeks*, but some *never fully adapt*.

slides.label: The risks
slides.text: Researchers have tied the weeks around both clock changes to more *mood problems*, more traffic accidents and *higher suicide risk*, according to the Sleep Foundation.

slides.label: The bill
slides.text: The House passed the *Sunshine Protection Act* on July 14 to make daylight saving time permanent. The Senate has *not acted*, so the clocks fall back as usual.

slides.label: The twist
slides.text: Sleep scientists want to stop switching too, but to *permanent standard time*. The AASM says it lines up better with the *body's internal clock*. Permanent DST fans cite more evening daylight.

slides.label: Winter blues
slides.text: Seasonal affective disorder usually starts in late fall and symptoms can last *four to five months*. NIMH says it is more common farther north: *New England more than Florida*.

slides.label: What helps
slides.text: NIMH points to *light therapy*, talk therapy and medication. The Sleep Foundation's basics: *morning light*, a steady wake time, less late caffeine, no alcohol before bed. In crisis, call or text *988*.

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: Sleep is not a weakness. It is the *base layer* under everything else. Sunday is a *free reset*, and a reminder to check on people who go quiet in winter. Not medical advice.

caption_linkedin:
Sunday's clock change is a good moment to treat sleep as a performance issue, not a personal failing.

The CDC, citing the AASM and Sleep Research Society, says adults 18 to 60 need at least seven hours a night, and more than a third of American adults regularly fall short. The Sleep Foundation notes that while the fall shift is gentler than spring, some people never fully adapt, and researchers link the weeks around clock changes to more mood problems and traffic accidents.

Policy is unsettled. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act on July 14 to make daylight saving time permanent, while the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and other groups back permanent standard time. For employers, the darker months are a reason to look at scheduling, shift work and how teams talk about seasonal mood.
